title: Leaving school for Detroit and the Bandbox
summary: He leaves in the eleventh grade for his uncle's grocery in Detroit, and gets gigs at the Bandbox musicians' club where older players test him.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: In fact, I left school in the Eleventh Grade. My Uncle, (?) Bernard(?) Reed and his wife, who was like my second mother, Lydia, they moved to Detroit. And as soon as he got himself going pretty well, anybody from home who wanted to come to Detroit, who figured they had a better chance...and he was sending for them. So he sent for me, and I went there, and I worked in his grocery store, and I started finding my way around.

It was during the summer when I went there, in 1940. And I started going down to the Bandbox, which was the musicians' club, where musicians would come in and hang out. And they had a piano there, and the guys would sit around and jam until the phone rang, then one of those leaders would go answer the phone, and he'd come and say, 'Well, I need a trumpet, I need a saxophone, I need a drummer, blah-blah-blah-blah' -- that's now you got gigs. So I was giggin'...got gigs that way around Detroit on the weekends.

And I met a lot of people there, especially one guy, a very fine friend of mine... At that time he was called Big Bill Moore; now they call him Wild Bill Moore. A saxophonist. I imagine you're familiar with him. And I'll talk about him later on in our California period, you know. But I was sixteen years old, you know, and I was a pretty fly little guy, you know. And the older guys, they would really put you through the test. During that time, "Liza" and "Tea For Two" and "Body and Soul," those were the tough numbers that they would play, you know. And we would play, and they would take me through all the keys with them and everything. But I was staying pretty sharp, because I was practicing hard, and really, really working on my instrument.
